extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, advertisers, political operatives, organizers, and institutional communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on planning and executing propaganda/public-relations campaigns: how to create events, choose media, enlist leaders, and ethically shape public opinion across commercial, political, educational and cultural domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of modern propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern propaganda is a consistent, enduring effort to create or shape events to influence the relations of the public to an enterprise, idea or group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat propaganda as active event-creation, not merely messaging; it applies to politics, charity, business, education and any large undertaking. Examples: creating publicity for a bond issue, marketing a picture, electing a president.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical criterion — merit and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether propaganda is good or bad depends upon the merit of the cause urged, and the correctness of the information published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda is legitimate when it disseminates truthful information in support of a cause judged beneficial; it is reprehensible when authors knowingly publish lies or aim at effects prejudicial to the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social anatomy and group loyalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda must take account of the anatomy of society, with its interlocking group formations and loyalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and map social, political, economic, racial, religious and professional cleavages; design appeals and channels suited to each group rather than treating the public as homogeneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target group leaders and key influencers
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure the cooperation of the key men in every group — persons whose mere word carried authority to hundreds or thousands of followers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enlist respected leaders, spokesmen, editors, clergy, professional presidents, and other authoritative figures to amplify and legitimize the message; use these leaders to reach their membership and constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances and events (event-based propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda often consists of creating circumstances and of creating pictures in the minds of millions of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan staged or genuine events that can be reported as news (e.g., fashion presentations, parades, expert lectures, demonstrations). Ensure events have credible sources/participants to gain editorial pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained, continuous, systematic effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is universal and continuous; it must be a consistent, enduring effort rather than a one-off initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain long-term campaigns and follow-up; small intelligent minorities must work continuously and systematically to change mass opinion. Short bursts without reinforcement will have limited effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit mental clichés and emotional habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective propaganda makes use of the mental clichés and the emotional habits of the public to produce mass reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft messages that fit existing stereotypes, habits and emotional triggers to facilitate rapid adoption; exercise ethical caution to avoid manipulating prejudices destructively (example: wartime atrocity appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness and editorial competition
rubrics_metrics.description: What the newspaper prints is governed by news value; created events must compete in the editorial office with other events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design publicity that satisfies editors' criteria for news (timeliness, significance, interest). Present factual, source-attributed material that can legitimately be seen as news rather than pure advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source transparency and factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of the news offered to the editor should always be clearly stated and the facts accurately presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never obscure provenance or invent facts; editors may discard items lacking credible sources. Accuracy preserves long-term credibility and increases chances of editorial pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match message to medium (medium-specific strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media have different functions: newspapers aim at news value; magazines follow continuous editorial policies; radio, motion pictures, lectures and personalities each have distinct propagandistic roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select channels appropriate to the message: use newspapers for timely events, magazines for themed campaigns, radio/film for mass standardization, lectures for thought-leadership (but ensure amplification), and personalities for human identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to changing relative value of media
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative value of the various instruments of propaganda, and their relation to the masses, are constantly changing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor technological and cultural shifts (e.g., automobile, radio, movies, television) and be ready to exploit new media and changing audience habits promptly to maintain reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage magazines' specialty orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines tend to propagate particular ideas according to their continuous policy (e.g., beauty, fashion, health).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch content that aligns with a magazine's theme and audience; arrange series or expert features that magazines can adopt as part of ongoing policy rather than one-off ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture value lies in repercussion
rubrics_metrics.description: The real value of the lecture, from the propaganda point of view, is in its repercussion to the general public (broadcasts, press reports, discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When organizing lectures, plan for subsequent media coverage or broadcasts to multiply impact; a lecture to a small audience can still be valuable if it is amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality management and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The public instinctively demands a personality to typify a conspicuous corporation or enterprise; a public figure must present an outward picture consistent with his real character and aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate and manage public personalities deliberately; avoid inconsistent or ludicrous publicity that undermines credibility. Treat personality as an objective asset to be aligned with organizational goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cultural and educational institutions as interpreters
rubrics_metrics.description: Museums, schools and universities should interpret their material to the public and project standards through lectures, loan collections, outreach, and applied-art programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop programs that bring institutional meaning into community life (e.g., museum councils of art, loan exhibits, story hours), and measure success not just by visitors but by public penetration and educational merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate scientific and technical ideas accessibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial and scientific advances must be interpreted to the public so inventions and discoveries can be understood and accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, candid explanations (charts, demonstrations, school materials) that make innovations intelligible; ensure educational institutions approve on educational merits to avoid charges of undue commercial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize strategy with skilled specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an increasing tendency to concentrate the functions of propaganda in the hands of the propaganda specialist or public-relations counsel due to expense and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ or coordinate specialist counsel to plan cross-media strategy, enlist influencers, and manage long-term campaigns rather than ad-hoc or fragmented efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motion pictures as mass-standardizers
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion picture is the greatest unconscious carrier of propaganda and can standardize the ideas and habits of a nation because it reflects and amplifies popular tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use film to reinforce prevailing trends and to reach large audiences broadly; remember films tend to exploit marketable ideas already in vogue rather than create wholly new opinions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be candid when integrating corporate material into education
rubrics_metrics.description: If a commercial concern supplies schools with material (e.g., how bread is made), such propaganda activities are not reprehensible if accurate and candid and accepted on educational merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer factual, non-misleading educational content and submit it to school authorities for vetting; avoid covert commercial promotion that lacks clear educational justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate editorial independence and possible rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors determine independently what is news and may kill stories they deem not to serve their readers' interests or to be tainted; the newspaper's obligation is to news and accuracy, not to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare materials that have clear public interest and news value; expect some editorial gatekeeping and avoid assuming publication is automatic simply because material is crafted as publicity.
